source_text:
ἢ τοὐναντίον ἐφύγετε
λαθόντες; Εἰ μὲν οὖν ὑμεῖς οἷοί· τε ἐγένεσθε τὸ τῆς πλάνης διαδρᾶναι πόμα, πρόδηλοι πολλοί τινες· εἰ δὲ τὸν κοινὸν πᾶσιν ἀέρα σπασάμενοι, τὸ τῆς λήθης ὕδωρ ἐπίετε χανδόν, πῶς καὶ πόθεν μυθοποιεῖτε λαβόντες περὶ ψυχῶν; πόθεν ὅλως ἴστε τὸ τῶν ῥείθρων τούτων γένος; εἴτε γὰρ μὴ ἐπειράθητε τῆς χρείας αὐτῶν, ἀγνοεῖτε τὴν τῶν ὑδάτων ἀνάδοσιν· εἴτε τῆς πείρας αὐτῶν ἔσω γεγονότες, λήθῃ τὴν μνήμην τῆς χρήσεως αὐτῶν ἠφανίσατε καὶ τὴν γνῶσιν ἐξεπτύσατε. Ἀλλ' εἰς ταῦτα βαρβαρώδη δεισιδαιμονίᾳ τραπέντες ἐσφάλησαν, Αἰγυπτίοις χρησάμενοι καθηγεμόσιν. 4 Ὅτι μὲν οὔκ εἰσιν ἀγέννητοι αἱ ψυχαὶ, τοῦτο δείκνυσιν σαφέστερον ἡ τῶν ἀρτιγόνων ἡλικία βρεφῶν.
thought_title: Dilemma of the water of forgetfulness
orientation: Eustathius is addressing the Pythagoreans and Platonists directly, pressing them on whether they themselves drank the mythical water of forgetfulness.
pass_a_gloss: Or the opposite: did you flee and escape notice? If then you were able to escape the water of forgetfulness, many others are clearly evident. But if, having drawn in the common air for all, you drank the water of forgetfulness greedily, how and from what source do you, having received it, fabricate myths about souls? From what source at all do you know the kind of these streams? For if you did not experience their use, you are ignorant of the rising of the waters. Or if you have been inside their experience, by forgetfulness you destroyed the memory of their use and spat out the knowledge. But having turned to these things with barbarous superstition, they went astray, having used Egyptians as guides. That the souls are not unbegotten, this the age of newborn infants shows more clearly.

choices.english: to escape the drink of deception
choices.why: Keeps the genitive of πλάνη as 'of deception' to preserve the source's characterization of the water as deceptive, and renders διαδρᾶναι as 'escape' to convey the sense of slipping away from it.
rejected: to flee from the drink of error
to run away from the draught of wandering

choices.english: having drawn in the common air for all
choices.why: Renders σπασάμενοι as 'having drawn in' to capture the physical act of breathing, and keeps 'common air for all' to preserve the dative πᾶσιν.
rejected: having inhaled the air common to all
having breathed the air shared by all

choices.why: The adverb conveys drinking in large gulps or without restraint, matching the contemptuous tone of the dilemma.
ἀνάδοσις means a giving up or emission from below, so 'rising' preserves the image of the waters welling up from their source.
The verb is vivid and physical; 'spat out' keeps the force of rejection and loss of the knowledge.
ἀρτίγονος means just-born; 'newborn infants' renders the phrase plainly and keeps the emphasis on the earliest stage of life.
rejected: the age of newly born babies

pass_b_english: Or the opposite: did you flee and escape notice? If you were able to escape the water of forgetfulness, then clearly many others were too. But if you drew in the common air that belongs to all and drank the water of forgetfulness in gulps, how and from what source do you fabricate myths about souls? How do you know at all the kind of these streams? For if you did not experience their use, you are ignorant of the dispensing of the waters. But if you were within the experience of them, you destroyed the memory of their use by forgetfulness and spat out the knowledge. Yet you turned to these things with barbaric superstition and went astray, using Egyptians as guides. That souls are not unbegotten is shown more clearly by the age of infants just born.

problems.why: Glossary fixes 'infant' for βρέφος, but 'newborn' is banned for βρέφος per glossary. The phrase 'newborn infants' uses banned term 'newborn' for βρέφος.
problems.fix: the age of infants just born

problems.quote: drank the water of forgetfulness greedily
problems.why: χανδόν means 'in gulps, copiously, to excess'—the manner of drinking, not greed as motive. 'Greedily' imposes a moral judgment absent in source.
problems.fix: drank the water of forgetfulness in gulps
problems.ruling: χανδόν = 'in gulps/copiously' (manner); 'greedily' adds moral motive absent in source, misleading reader.

problems.why: ἀνάδοσιν here means 'dispensing, distribution, giving out' (of waters), not 'rising.' The philosophers don't know the waters exist if they didn't experience them.
problems.ruling: ἀνάδοσιν = 'dispensing/distribution'; 'rising' changes meaning—context is waters being given out, not rising.

edits.old: drank the water of forgetfulness greedily
edits.new: drank the water of forgetfulness in gulps
the age of infants just born

fixed: Changed 'greedily' to 'in gulps' to match χανδόν as manner of drinking, not motive.
Changed 'newborn infants' to 'infants just born' to avoid banned term 'newborn' for βρέφος.

problems.quote: Yet they turned to these things with barbaric superstition and went astray, using Egyptians as guides.
problems.source_quote: Ἀλλ' εἰς ταῦτα βαρβαρώδη δεισιδαιμονίᾳ τραπέντες ἐσφάλησαν, Αἰγυπτίοις χρησάμενοι καθηγεμόσιν.
problems.why: English "they" hides Eustathius's direct address; the Greek continues second-person plural (τραπέντες), referring to the philosophers.
problems.fix: Yet you turned to these things with barbaric superstition and went astray, using Egyptians as guides.
problems.ruling: Greek τραπέντες/ἐσφάλησαν are 2nd pl., addressing opponents directly; 'they' shifts to 3rd person, misleading reader.

edits.old: Yet they turned to these things with barbaric superstition and went astray, using Egyptians as guides.
edits.new: Yet you turned to these things with barbaric superstition and went astray, using Egyptians as guides.

problems.quote: But if you drew in the common air
problems.why: Rhetorical questions to opponents blend with author's own assertions; voice shifts unclear
problems.fix: Indicate direct address to Pythagoreans/Platonists continues

problems.why: Same mythic drink called two different names; reader may think two separate things.

edits.old: But if you drew in the common air that belongs to all and drank the water of forgetfulness in gulps, how and from what source do you fabricate myths about souls?
edits.new: But if you drew in the common air that belongs to all and drank the water of forgetfulness in gulps, how and from what source do you fabricate myths about souls, Pythagoreans and Platonists?

fixed: Speaker: Added direct address to Pythagoreans and Platonists to clarify the rhetorical question continues.
Glossary: Unified the mythic drink as 'water of forgetfulness' throughout.

problems.quote: the common air that belongs to all
problems.why: False variant—ignore. Actually: 'air' vs 'water' in same sentence is deliberate contrast, not drift.

variants.text: the common air that belongs to all
drank the water of forgetfulness in gulps

problems.quote: But if you drew in the common air that belongs to all
problems.why: Rhetorical question to Pythagoreans/Platonists, but 'common air' is ambiguous—literal breathing or metaphor?
problems.fix: Clarify this is sarcastic: 'if you merely breathed ordinary air.'

edits.old: But if you drew in the common air that belongs to all and drank the water of forgetfulness in gulps
edits.new: But if you merely breathed ordinary air and drank the water of forgetfulness in gulps

fixed: The 'common air' phrase is not a false variant; it is a deliberate contrast with the water of forgetfulness. However, the English was ambiguous, so I clarified it as sarcastic: 'merely breathed ordinary air.'
The speaker issue is resolved by the same clarification, which makes the rhetorical sarcasm to Pythagoreans and Platonists clearer.

last_rejected.quote: the common air that belongs to all
last_rejected.why: κοινὸν πᾶσιν means 'common to all', not 'belongs to all'; but worse, ἀήρ here means 'breath' or 'vapor', not 'air' as element—it's the breath/vapor of the waters, a poetic/mythic reference.
last_rejected.ruling: κοινὸν πᾶσιν = 'common to all'; 'belongs to all' is equivalent. ἀήρ can mean 'air'; no meaning lost.

last_rejected.why: ἀνάδοσιν means 'giving up', 'yielding', or 'springing forth' (of waters from a source), not 'dispensing' as if someone distributes them; it's about the waters' origin/flow.
last_rejected.fix: the rising or springing forth of the waters
last_rejected.ruling: ἀνάδοσιν can mean 'dispensing/supplying' of waters; within normal range, no meaning changed.

last_rejected.quote: were within the experience of them
last_rejected.why: ἔσω γεγονότες τῆς πείρας means 'having come inside/within the experience', i.e., having actually experienced them; 'were within' is awkward and obscures that they underwent the experience.
last_rejected.fix: having entered into experience of them
last_rejected.ruling: ἔσω γεγονότες = 'were within'; context implies experiencing. Awkward but not a major error.
